svg.text: Figure 9 - Inline system ECC lives in the same open row
Two of the 32 columns in every row hold the check bits for the other 30. Fetching ECC therefore costs one column access - no activate, no precharge.
E0
E1
ECC column 30 protects data columns 0 - 14
15 blocks x 16 check bits = 240 of 256 bits used
ECC column 31 protects data columns 15 - 29
code is (272,256): single 4-bit symbol correct, double detect
ECC column cache
32 entries x 32 B = 1 KB per pseudo-channel
DIRECT-MAPPED BY BANK INDEX - no tags, no replacement policy
This is exact, not an approximation: a bank has ONE open row,
and each row-half has ONE ECC column, so there is never more
than one ECC block per bank in flight.
Write-allocate elision
Each cache entry carries 15 field-valid bits.
If a write stream fills all 15 before eviction, the ECC block is
GENERATED, never read. No read-modify-write on the write path.
This is what keeps writes at 6.25% instead of 12.5%.
Cost, stated honestly
Capacity 2/32 = 6.25% (240 GB usable of 256 GB) Bandwidth 6.25% sequential read AND write
6.25% of 8.19 TB/s is 512 GB/s. That is the floor for this class of scheme, and it is cheap next to a wrong answer.
What Rev 0.1 got wrong (kept here because the failure mode is instructive)
It put the ECC block in a different ROW of the same bank. A bank has one row buffer, so every ECC fetch would have
precharged the row being streamed and re-activated it after: ~60 ns each, ~12.5% overhead, and double the ACT rate against tFAW.
One DRAM row, one bank, one pseudo-channel (1 KB = 32 columns of 32 B)
columns 0 .. 29 = DATA
cols 30, 31 = ECC
